conversations.answer: PlanFrom the task, it is clear that we need to separate the interactive and web sessions, and move the common parts to a separate module. The common parts here seem to be creating a prompt and saving it, which are both done before sending it via API. Therefore, we can create a new module named promptProcessing.js that will handle these tasks.The promptProcessing.js will contain a single exported function named processPrompt that takes in a string command, last_command_result, saveto location, and parent_message_id, and outputs the processed prompt and parent_message_id.Then, we will modify the startInteractiveSession.js file and server.js file to use the processPrompt function from promptProcessing.js.In the server.js file, we will remove the saveAndSendPrompt function because the API shouldn't be called yet. Instead, it will use the processPrompt function from promptProcessing.js to generate the prompt.Lastly, we will adjust the saveAndSendPrompt.js function to call the processPrompt function and then call the API.Shell Script[CODE_BLOCK_0]The bash script above should fix the error and separate the interactive and web sessions by extracting the common parts into a separate module promptProcessing.js. It modifies startInteractiveSession.js, server.js and saveAndSendPrompt.js to accommodate these changes. The web interface now should not call the API, but instead, just return the processed prompt.

conversations.answer: The error suggests that you are trying to assign a value to a constant variable (parent_message_id). Constants are block-scoped, much like variables defined using let keyword. The value of a constant cannot change through re-assignment, and a constant cannot be re-declared.Since we want to change the value of parent_message_id after the API sends the message, it should be declared with let instead of const.Here is how to fix it:[CODE_BLOCK_0]This script rewrites the saveAndSendPrompt.js file and changes the declaration of parent_message_id from const to let. This way, you can reassign the value of parent_message_id with the ID of the sent message (res.id). The same applies to prompt and lastTextLength.

conversations.answer: To render the generated prompts as markdown on your website, you will need to use a markdown parser that can convert markdown into HTML that your web application can render.There are several libraries available that can help you with this, including marked, remark, showdown, and more. Here is an example using marked:First, install the marked library by running:[CODE_BLOCK_0]Then, you can import marked in your server code and use it to convert the prompt to HTML before sending it in the response:[CODE_BLOCK_1]In the script above, marked(prompt) converts the markdown in prompt to HTML. The htmlPrompt is then sent as part of the response. On your frontend, you will render this HTML to display the prompt in markdown format. Make sure to sanitize the HTML if needed depending on your frontend framework or library.Please note that you also need to handle the markdown rendering in the frontend of your web application. Ensure that the HTML is rendered properly in your frontend framework (React, Vue, Angular, etc.).

conversations.prompt: Now I see html, but not parsed by the browser. Change the jsx please!
conversations.answer: When returning HTML from an API to be rendered on a front end application, it's important to keep in mind that for security reasons, most front-end frameworks (like React, Vue, etc.) do not render raw HTML out of the box.However, since you're using an Express server and you want to display the HTML directly, you may want to consider using a templating engine (like Pug, EJS, or Handlebars), or serving static HTML files. Alternatively, if you're looking to inject this HTML directly into a single page application (SPA), you'll need to handle the HTML rendering on the client-side, in the JavaScript of your SPA.Assuming you're using React for your frontend, you can use dangerouslySetInnerHTML to render HTML strings:[CODE_BLOCK_0]Just replace yourHTMLString with the variable that contains the HTML you received from the server.Please note that using dangerouslySetInnerHTML can open up your site to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks if misused, hence the name "dangerously". This is why it's crucial to ensure the HTML content you're inserting is properly sanitized and trusted. Be careful when using this approach, and only use it when necessary.Given that the backend service you're developing is separate from the frontend, it's the frontend's responsibility to handle how the HTML is rendered. The backend simply provides the data (HTML, in this case). As such, you would not typically handle this within your Express server or server.js file. Instead, this would be done in the client-side code.
